title: 22. Interview: Design Uber
summary: Interview Q&A for Design Uber — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Design Uber interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Trade-offs Discussed
sections.body:
- **Geohash vs S2 vs H3**: geohash is simplest (string prefix), but has edge cases at the equator and cell boundaries. Google S2 (sphere-based) handles boundaries better and supports arbitrary cell sizes. Uber H3 (hexagonal) is best for neighbor queries (every hex has 6 equidistant neighbors) but is more complex. We pick Redis GEO (geohash-backed) for simplicity, with S2 as a fallback index.
- **Dispatch: nearest-driver vs supply-demand-balanced**: nearest-driver is fast and simple but can leave some areas underserved. Supply-demand dispatch (send driver to where demand is high) is better long-term but complex. We pick nearest-driver for the immediate match + surge pricing for the long-term balance.
- **Driver timeout: 15 s vs 5 s**: 15 s gives the driver time to read the offer; 5 s reduces rider wait. We pick 15 s with parallel offers to the next 2 candidates (pre-fetched) so the next match is instant on decline.
- **Push vs WebSocket for driver offers**: push (APNS/FCM) is reliable but slow (5–10 s delivery). WebSocket is instant but requires an active connection. We pick WebSocket for the offer (driver app is foreground), with push as fallback if WebSocket is dead.
- **Surge: per-cell vs per-city**: per-cell (1.2 km) is precise but can fluctuate wildly between adjacent cells. Per-city is stable but overapplies surge to underserved areas. We pick per-cell with smoothing (weighted average of neighbors).
- **Strong vs eventual consistency for driver status**: strong (Redis SETNX) ensures no double-match but adds latency. Eventual (Cassandra) is faster but risks double-match. We pick strong for the dispatch-critical driver_status (Redis); eventual for everything else.

sections.title: Q1. How does Uber's dispatch system find the nearest driver within 3 seconds?
sections.body:
**Answer:** The dispatch algorithm has four stages. (1) **Geospatial query**: the rider's pickup location is queried against Redis GEO (a sorted set backed by geohash) using `GEORADIUS` to find the nearest N available drivers within radius R (typically 3 km). This query takes < 5 ms. (2) **Filtering**: each candidate's status is checked in Redis (`driver_status:{id}`) — busy or offline drivers are removed. (3) **ETA fetch**: for each remaining candidate, the dispatch service calls the ETA service to predict driving time (not straight-line distance) from driver to pickup. This is the slowest step (~50 ms per call), so it's parallelized across candidates. (4) **Driver offer**: the dispatch service picks the closest driver (by ETA, not distance), sends a WebSocket push to the driver's app with the offer (pickup, destination, fare, ETA), and waits 15 s for acceptance. If declined or timeout, dispatch moves to the next candidate (pre-fetched ETAs make this instant). The total budget: 5 ms (Redis) + 50 ms (ETA) + 15 s (driver timeout) + small overhead = well under the 3-s p99 target for the *system* response (the 15-s driver timeout is rider-visible wait, but the system has matched in < 1 s). Real-world: Uber's dispatch uses this architecture, with Redis GEO replaced by their custom geospatial index (DISCO), but the principles are the same.
**Visual:**
```
1. Redis GEORADIUS pickup 3 km COUNT 10 ASC  (< 5 ms)
   -> [(driver_42, 0.8km), (driver_17, 1.2km), ...]
2. Filter: check driver_status in Redis (< 5 ms)
   -> remove busy/offline drivers
3. ETA fetch (parallel, ~50 ms)
   -> for each candidate: ETA service(driver_loc, pickup)
4. Driver offer (15 s timeout)
   -> WebSocket push to closest driver
   -> if accept: match; if decline/timeout: next candidate
   -> next candidate ETAs already pre-fetched -> instant retry

Total system response: < 1s (excluding 15s driver timeout)
```

sections.title: Q2. How does surge pricing work, and why doesn't it just go to infinity?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Surge pricing is dynamic pricing based on real-time supply/demand in a geofenced area. (1) **Demand**: count open ride requests in a geohash cell over the last 5 min (Kafka stream of `trip-requested` events). (2) **Supply**: count available drivers in that cell (Redis GEO query). (3) **Ratio**: `surge = max(1.0, min(3.0, 1.5 / max(ratio, 0.1)))` — when supply > demand (ratio > 1.5), surge = 1.0× (no surge); when demand >> supply (ratio < 0.5), surge approaches 3.0× (cap). (4) **Smoothing**: surge is averaged with neighboring cells to prevent wild fluctuations between adjacent areas. (5) **Recomputation**: every 5 min per cell; cached in Redis with 10-min TTL. **Why it doesn't go to infinity**: (a) hard cap at 3.0× (Uber's policy — higher surge triggers user abandonment); (b) higher surge incentivizes more drivers to come online (supply increases, ratio improves, surge drops); (c) smoothing prevents spikes; (d) the cap can be raised during emergencies (Halloween, New Year's Eve) but generally stays at 3.0×. Trade-off: surge is unpopular with riders but necessary — without it, demand exceeds supply and riders wait 30+ min. Surge redistributes demand (some riders wait) and supply (more drivers come online). Real-world: Uber's surge is described in their engineering blog; the algorithm has been refined since 2014.
**Visual:**
```
Per geofenced cell (geohash6, ~1.2km):
  Demand  = open trip requests in last 5 min (Kafka stream)
  Supply  = available drivers in cell (Redis GEO)
  Ratio   = Supply / Demand

  Surge = clamp(1.5 / max(ratio, 0.1), min=1.0, max=3.0)
        + smoothing (avg with neighbor cells)

  ratio=3.0  -> surge=1.0x (plenty of supply)
  ratio=1.0  -> surge=1.5x
  ratio=0.5  -> surge=3.0x (capped)

Why it doesn't go to infinity:
  1. Hard cap 3.0x (Uber policy)
  2. Higher surge -> more drivers come online -> supply up -> surge drops
  3. Smoothing prevents spikes
  4. Cap raised only for known events (Halloween, NYE)
```

sections.title: Q3. Why does Uber use Kafka as the event backbone, and what events flow through it?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Kafka is the durable, replayable event log that ties Uber's microservices together. Uber has ~2 000 microservices; they can't all talk to each other directly (that would be O(N²) point-to-point integrations). Kafka provides a publish-subscribe model: services publish events to topics; consumers subscribe to the topics they care about. **Key event topics**. (1) `driver-location-updates`: 1.7 M/s globally — every driver ping (lat, lon, heading, speed, status). Consumers: geolocation service (updates Redis GEO), map matching service (snaps GPS to roads), ETA model (real-time traffic), surge calculator. (2) `trip-events`: ride-requested, matched, en-route, pickup, in-progress, drop-off, completed, canceled. Consumers: payment service, notification service, rating service, analytics. (3) `surge-updates`: per-cell surge multiplier updates every 5 min. Consumers: pricing service, rider app (for fare estimates). (4) `driver-status-changes`: online, busy, offline. Consumers: dispatch service, analytics. **Why Kafka**: (a) durability (events survive consumer crashes); (b) replayability (re-process old events for new consumers or bug fixes); (c) decoupling (producers don't know about consumers); (d) horizontal scalability (partition by `driver_id` or `trip_id` for parallel consumption); (e) ordering guarantees per partition. Trade-off: Kafka adds operational complexity (cluster management, schema registry), but the decoupling benefit is essential at Uber's scale. Real-world: Uber has written extensively about their Kafka migration (from a custom pub-sub to Kafka) and now processes trillions of events/day.
**Visual:**
```
~2000 microservices -> can't talk point-to-point (O(N^2))

Kafka topics (decoupled pub-sub):
  driver-location-updates (1.7M/s)
    -> Geolocation svc (Redis GEO)
    -> Map matching svc (HMM)
    -> ETA model (traffic)
    -> Surge calculator
  trip-events (200/s)
    -> Payment svc, Notification svc, Rating svc, Analytics
  surge-updates (3300/s)
    -> Pricing svc, Rider app (fare estimates)
  driver-status-changes
    -> Dispatch svc, Analytics

Benefits: durable, replayable, decoupled, scalable, ordered per partition
```

sections.title: Q4. How does geospatial indexing work, and why geohash vs S2 vs H3?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Geospatial indexing is the data structure that supports "find nearest N drivers within radius R" queries. Three main approaches. (1) **Geohash**: encode (lat, lon) as a base-32 string where prefix sharing = geographic proximity. E.g., `dr5regw` (Manhattan) and `dr5regx` (also Manhattan) share the first 6 chars. Redis GEO uses geohash internally (stored as a sorted set). Pros: simple, well-supported in Redis. Cons: cells have variable sizes (longer near poles), edge cases at the equator and antimeridian. (2) **Google S2**: a hierarchical decomposition of the sphere into cells. Each cell is a quadrilateral bounded by great-circle arcs. Pros: handles sphere geometry correctly, supports arbitrary cell sizes (level 0 = whole Earth, level 30 = 1 cm²), neighbor queries are well-defined. Cons: more complex to learn and implement. (3) **Uber H3**: hexagonal grid. Pros: every hex has exactly 6 equidistant neighbors (unlike squares which have 4 edge + 4 corner neighbors with different distances), better for radius queries. Cons: more complex; hexagons don't tile perfectly at all resolutions. **Uber's choice**: H3 for analytics and surge (neighbor queries matter); Redis GEO (geohash) for the real-time driver index (simplicity, sub-ms queries). **Trade-off**: at scale, the choice matters for edge cases (e.g., drivers near cell boundaries). H3 is the most theoretically correct; geohash is the simplest. Real-world: Uber open-sourced H3 in 2018; it's now used by many geospatial applications.
**Visual:**
```
Geohash (Redis GEO):
  dr5regw (Manhattan block A)
  dr5regx (Manhattan block B)  -> prefix share = nearby
  Simple, sub-ms GEORADIUS queries
  Cons: variable cell sizes, pole edge cases

S2 (Google):
  Hierarchical sphere decomposition
  Levels 0-30 (1cm^2 to whole Earth)
  Pros: correct sphere geometry
  Cons: complex

H3 (Uber):
  Hexagonal grid
  Every hex has 6 equidistant neighbors
  Best for radius/neighbor queries
  Used by Uber for surge + analytics

Uber's mix:
  Real-time driver index: Redis GEO (geohash) - simplicity
  Analytics + surge:      H3 - neighbor correctness
```

sections.title: Q5. How does Uber ensure a driver isn't matched to two riders simultaneously?
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is a critical consistency problem — a double-match is a serious bug (driver shows up for one rider, other rider is stranded). Three layers of defense. (1) **Redis atomic SETNX**: when a driver accepts a ride, the dispatch service runs `SETNX driver_status:{id} busy` (set if not exists). The first call succeeds (returns 1); subsequent calls fail (returns 0). This is an atomic Redis operation, so even concurrent dispatch services can't both succeed. (2) **Remove from GEO index**: on accept, `ZREM drivers:online {driver_id}` removes the driver from the geospatial index. Subsequent `GEORADIUS` queries won't find this driver. (3) **Trip state machine**: the trip transitions `requested → matched`, and the state machine service validates that the trip is still in `requested` state before transitioning. If another dispatch already matched it, the transition fails. (4) **Optimistic locking**: the trip's `version` field is checked on update — if it changed since the dispatch read it, the update is rejected. (5) **Idempotency keys**: the rider's `POST /trips` request has an idempotency key; duplicates return the same trip_id. **Edge case**: what if the driver accepts at the exact millisecond the rider cancels? The trip's state machine: if the rider's cancel request arrives first, the trip is `canceled` and the driver's accept is rejected. If the driver's accept arrives first, the trip is `matched` and the rider's cancel is rejected (the rider must cancel via the app and pay a fee). Real-world: Uber's engineering blog has described these patterns; the Redis SETNX + GEO ZREM combo is the core mechanism.
**Visual:**
```
Driver accepts ride at time T:
  1. Redis SETNX driver_status:{id} busy
       -> returns 1 (first accept) or 0 (already busy)
       -> atomic, prevents double-match
  2. Redis ZREM drivers:online {driver_id}
       -> removes from GEO index, no future dispatch finds them
  3. Trip state machine: requested -> matched
       -> validates trip is still 'requested' before transition
  4. Optimistic locking: trip.version check on update
  5. Idempotency key on POST /trips (duplicates return same trip_id)

Edge case: driver accepts at same millisecond as rider cancels
  -> whichever request first wins (state machine is the arbiter)
```

sections.title: Q6. How does map matching work, and why is it needed?
sections.body:
**Answer:** GPS pings from a phone are noisy — typically ±10–20 m error, worse in urban canyons ( skyscrapers reflect signals) and tunnels (no signal). If you plotted raw GPS pings on a map, the driver would appear to drive through buildings, jump between parallel streets, and teleport. Map matching is the algorithm that snaps these noisy pings to the actual road network. **The algorithm**: Uber uses a Hidden Markov Model (HMM), based on the Newson & Krumm 2009 paper. (1) **States**: each road segment (edge in the road graph) is a state. (2) **Observations**: each GPS ping is an observation. (3) **Emission probability**: how likely is this ping given the road segment? Higher if the ping is close to the road. Modeled as `exp(-distance / sigma)` where sigma ≈ 20 m. (4) **Transition probability**: how likely is it to transition from road A to road B between two pings? Higher if the road-network distance between A and B matches the GPS distance between the two pings. Modeled as `exp(-|gps_dist - road_dist| / beta)` where beta ≈ 50 m. (5) **Viterbi algorithm**: find the most likely sequence of road segments given the observation sequence. The output: a snapped path along actual roads, plus confidence scores. **Why it matters**: (a) fare calculation (distance must be road distance, not GPS straight-line); (b) ETA prediction (which road is the driver on?); (c) rider experience (rider sees the driver on the actual road, not in a building); (d) fraud detection (a driver whose pings consistently mismatch roads may be spoofing). Real-world: Uber's map matching handles billions of pings/day; the HMM approach is industry-standard.
**Visual:**
```
Raw GPS pings (noisy, ±20m):
  *  *        *
        *   *
   ---------Road A---------  (actual road)
                *    *
  *  *  *  *
   ---------Road B---------  (parallel road, 30m away)

HMM map matching:
  States: road segments (A1, A2, A3, B1, B2, ...)
  Observations: GPS pings
  Emission:   P(ping | road) = exp(-gps_to_road_distance / 20)
  Transition: P(road_t | road_{t-1}) = exp(-|gps_dist - road_dist| / 50)

Viterbi: find most likely sequence of road segments
  -> snap pings to road A (highest probability path)
```

sections.title: Q7. How does Uber handle a driver's app losing connection mid-trip?
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is a common real-world scenario (driver enters a tunnel, loses signal). Three concerns. (1) **Driver status**: if no ping arrives for 30 s, the driver's status auto-expires (Redis TTL on `driver_status:{id}`). They'd appear offline — bad, because they're mid-trip. Solution: a separate `on_trip` flag with a longer TTL (5 min); drivers in `on_trip` state are never auto-offlined. (2) **Trip continuity**: the rider's app shows the driver's last known location, frozen. The rider sees a "driver's location may be delayed" warning. When the driver's connection returns, the app sends a burst of buffered pings (the app stores pings locally when offline); the rider's map "catches up" with a smooth animation. (3) **GPS track integrity**: the trip's GPS track in Cassandra has gaps during the outage. On reconnect, the app backfills from its local buffer. If the buffer is lost (app crash), the gap remains — the fare is calculated from the road-network distance between the last known point and the next point (map matching fills the gap). (4) **Payment**: payment is unaffected — it's based on the trip's recorded distance/time, not real-time pings. (5) **Driver safety check**: if a driver is mid-trip and offline for > 5 min, Uber's safety system sends a push notification ("Are you OK?"); if no response in 2 min, Uber calls the driver. (6) **Rider reassurance**: the rider gets a notification ("Driver is in an area with weak signal — they'll be there soon"). Real-world: Uber's app handles this gracefully; the architecture is described in their engineering blog.
**Visual:**
```
Driver enters tunnel, loses signal at T+5min:
  T+5:00 -> last ping received
  T+5:30 -> driver_status TTL would expire, BUT:
             on_trip flag has 5-min TTL -> driver stays "in trip"
  T+5:30 -> rider sees "location may be delayed" warning
  T+5:30+ -> app buffers pings locally on driver's phone
  T+6:00 -> driver exits tunnel, signal returns
  T+6:00 -> app sends burst of buffered pings to Kafka
  T+6:01 -> rider's map animates driver's path through the tunnel
  T+6:01 -> Cassandra backfills GPS track from buffer

If outage > 5 min:
  Safety system: push "Are you OK?" -> if no response in 2 min, call driver
```

sections.title: Q1. A rider reports no drivers are available in their area at 9 AM (rush hour). How do you…
sections.body:
**Answer:** Step-by-step. (1) **Verify with data**: check the geolocation service for the rider's area — how many drivers are actually online in the rider's geohash cell (and adjacent cells)? If 0 drivers, the issue is supply. If 50 drivers, the issue is dispatch or filtering. (2) **Driver supply**: check driver-online events in Kafka for that area over the last hour — did drivers go offline? Was there a sporting event that drew drivers elsewhere? Is surge too low to attract drivers? (3) **Surge multiplier**: check `surge:{cell}` in Redis — if it's 1.0× (no surge), drivers may be in adjacent cells with higher surge. Consider raising surge in the rider's cell to attract drivers. (4) **Dispatch radius**: check the dispatch service logs for the rider's request — what radius was searched? If only 3 km and drivers are 5 km away, expand the radius (or fall back to a "drivers nearby, ETA 10 min" message). (5) **Driver app health**: check driver app crash reports and WebSocket disconnection rates for that area — if drivers are dropping off due to app bugs, that's a different fix. (6) **Network/CDN**: is the rider's request even reaching the API gateway? Check API gateway logs for the rider's session. (7) **Geofencing/regulatory**: some cities (e.g., London, NYC) require special licensing — drivers without the right license are filtered out. Check filter logic. Most likely cause: low supply (drivers went to higher-surge adjacent areas) or app/network issues. Fix: raise surge in the rider's cell; if persistent, investigate driver app crashes.
**Visual:**
```
Rider: no drivers at 9 AM
  |
  +--> Geolocation svc: how many drivers online in cell? (0 vs 50?)
  |       0 -> supply issue; 50 -> dispatch/filter issue
  +--> Kafka driver-online events: drivers going offline? moving?
  +--> Surge in cell? -> if 1.0x, drivers in adjacent higher-surge cells
  +--> Dispatch radius searched? -> expand if only 3km
  +--> Driver app crashes/disconnects? -> check reports
  +--> Rider request reaching API? -> check gateway logs
  +--> Geofencing/licensing filter? -> some cities filter drivers
  Most likely: low supply -> raise surge to attract drivers
```

sections.title: Q2. The CEO wants to add UberPool (shared rides with multiple pickups). How does the…
sections.body:
**Answer:** UberPool is fundamentally harder than regular UberX — you're matching multiple riders to one driver along a route, optimizing for shared miles. (1) **Trip planning**: instead of a single (pickup, destination), the driver's trip has a sequence: pickup_A → pickup_B → dropoff_A → dropoff_B (or other orderings). The dispatch must find a driver whose current route passes near the new rider's pickup, and whose final destination is in the same general direction. (2) **Routing optimization**: a route-planning service solves the traveling salesman problem with time windows — given 2–3 riders, find the order that minimizes total miles + wait time. NP-hard in general, but solvable for small N with branch-and-bound. (3) **Matchmaking algorithm**: for a new ride request, find drivers currently in trip whose route passes near the new pickup (within ~5 min detour) AND whose existing rider's dropoff is in the same direction. (4) **Re-routing**: when a new rider joins, the driver's route updates; both riders see the updated ETA. (5) **Pricing**: Pool rides are cheaper (typically 30–50% less than UberX) because the cost is shared. Pricing service must compute per-rider fares based on their share of the route. (6) **Rider experience**: longer wait, longer ride (detours), but cheaper. (7) **Capacity**: a driver can take 2–4 Pool riders depending on vehicle size. (8) **Edge cases**: rider cancels mid-trip (re-route to skip their stop); driver needs a break; rider no-shows. Trade-off: Pool is operationally complex but increases driver utilization (more revenue per hour) and reduces cost for riders. Real-world: UberPool ran for years (now rebranded as UberX Share); the algorithm is described in their engineering blog.
**Visual:**
```
UberX: 1 rider -> 1 driver, simple A->B route
UberPool: N riders -> 1 driver, sequenced pickups/dropoffs

New Pool request (rider_B):
  1. Find drivers in trip whose route passes near rider_B's pickup (5-min detour)
  2. Check direction match: rider_B's dest near driver's route
  3. Route planning: solve TSP with time windows
       pickup_A -> pickup_B -> dropoff_A -> dropoff_B
       minimize total miles + wait time
  4. Re-route driver; update both riders' ETAs
  5. Price: rider_B pays share of route (30-50% cheaper than UberX)

Edge cases:
  - rider cancels -> re-route to skip their stop
  - rider no-show -> driver waits 2 min, then continues
  - 4 riders max (vehicle size limit)
```

sections.title: Q3. A driver reports they accepted a ride but the rider's location shows 2 km away (not where…
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is likely a GPS accuracy or app issue. (1) **Rider's actual location**: check the rider's app — what does it show as their pickup? The rider may have moved the pin manually (the app allows adjusting the pickup) but the saved location is different. (2) **GPS accuracy**: check the rider's last few GPS pings — were they accurate? In urban canyons or indoors, GPS can be off by 100+ m. The rider's app may have submitted a bad location. (3) **Address geocoding**: if the rider entered a text address ("123 Main St"), the geocoder may have placed it at the wrong location (e.g., a different "Main St" in another city). Check the geocoding service. (4) **Saved places**: if the rider used a saved place ("Home"), the saved coordinates may be stale (they moved). Check the saved-places service. (5) **Map matching**: was the rider's location snapped to the wrong road by map matching? Check the map-matching service logs for the rider's session. (6) **Driver's GPS**: alternatively, the driver's GPS may be wrong — they think they're at location X but they're actually at Y. Check the driver's recent pings. (7) **Network issue**: if the rider's app submitted the location over a slow connection, the location may be from 5 min ago (before they moved). Fix: have the rider open the app and verify their pickup pin; if it's wrong, they can adjust it. For drivers, the app should show the rider's actual GPS coordinates (not the geocoded address) so the driver can navigate precisely. Real-world: Uber's app shows both the geocoded address and the GPS pin; the driver navigates to the pin.
**Visual:**
```
Driver sees rider 2km away
  |
  +--> Rider's app: what does it show as pickup?
  |       (rider may have moved pin manually)
  +--> Rider's GPS pings accurate? (urban canyon, indoor)
  +--> Address geocoding correct? (wrong "Main St")
  +--> Saved place stale? (rider moved, "Home" not updated)
  +--> Map matching snapped wrong?
  +--> Driver's GPS wrong? (driver's pings off)
  +--> Network lag? (location is 5 min old)
  Fix: rider verifies pin in app; driver navigates to GPS pin, not address
```

sections.title: Q4. Surge pricing is showing 3.0× in a small area but 1.0× everywhere around it. How do you…
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is a surge smoothing or supply issue. (1) **Verify the surge value**: check Redis `surge:{cell}` for the rider's location — is it actually 3.0×? (2) **Demand in that cell**: check Kafka for `trip-requested` events in that cell over the last 5 min — is there a spike? (e.g., a concert just ended and 200 people requested rides simultaneously). (3) **Supply in that cell**: check Redis GEO for available drivers in that cell — is it 0? If 0 drivers and 200 requests, surge 3.0× is correct. (4) **Surge smoothing**: the surge algorithm averages a cell's raw surge with its neighbors. If smoothing isn't applied (or the smoothing window is too small), an isolated cell can spike to 3.0× while neighbors stay at 1.0×. Check the surge service config — is smoothing enabled? (5) **Geofence boundary**: if the cell is at a geofence boundary (e.g., a city border), the algorithm may treat it differently. (6) **Driver hoarding**: drivers in adjacent cells (1.0× surge) may be moving toward the 3.0× cell to capture the surge. Once they arrive, supply increases and surge should drop. Check driver movement patterns. (7) **Surge update lag**: surge is recomputed every 5 min — if the spike just happened, the next update will adjust. (8) **Manual surge override**: Uber's ops team can manually set surge in specific areas (e.g., during emergencies). Check if a manual override is in effect. Most likely cause: a localized demand spike (concert, train arrival) with smoothing not fully effective. Fix: enable tighter smoothing or wait for the next 5-min recompute.
**Visual:**
```
Surge 3.0x in one cell, 1.0x around it
  |
  +--> Verify Redis surge:{cell} = 3.0?
  +--> Demand spike? (Kafka trip-requested in last 5 min)
  |       e.g., concert ended, 200 requests
  +--> Supply in cell? (Redis GEO count = 0?)
  +--> Surge smoothing enabled? (avg with neighbors)
  |       if not, isolated cell can spike
  +--> Geofence boundary? (cell on city border)
  +--> Drivers moving toward cell? (will drop surge next cycle)
  +--> Surge recompute lag? (5-min cycle, will adjust)
  +--> Manual override by ops? (emergencies)
  Fix: enable smoothing or wait for recompute
```

sections.title: Q5. A rider reports they were charged for a trip they didn't take (their account was used in…
sections.body:
**Answer:** This is a fraud case. (1) **Trip details**: pull the trip record from Cassandra — what was the pickup, destination, time, driver, payment method? Confirm the rider's claim (was it really a trip they didn't take?). (2) **Device fingerprint**: check the device that requested the trip — device ID, IP, user-agent. Does it match the rider's usual device? If a different device requested the trip, the account was compromised (login credentials stolen). (3) **Login history**: check recent logins to the rider's account — were there logins from unfamiliar IPs or locations? (4) **Payment method**: was a new payment method added recently? Fraudsters often add a new card to a stolen account. (5) **Location mismatch**: the rider's claim is "I was in NYC, the trip was in London." Check the rider's recent location pings (their app sends pings even when not in a trip) — were they in NYC at the time? If yes, the trip was definitely not theirs. (6) **Driver's perspective**: contact the driver — did they pick up the rider whose photo matches the account? If the actual rider didn't match the account photo, it's confirmed fraud. (7) **Refund and remediation**: refund the rider immediately, mark the trip as fraudulent, ban the fraudulent device, force a password reset on the rider's account, and add 2FA requirement. (8) **Pattern analysis**: check if this is part of a broader attack — multiple accounts compromised from the same IP? Feed the fraud signals to the fraud detection model. Real-world: Uber has a dedicated fraud team; account takeovers are common and handled via this playbook.
**Visual:**
```
Rider: "I was charged for a trip I didn't take"
  |
  +--> Trip record: pickup, dest, time, driver, payment
  +--> Device fingerprint: matches rider's usual device?
  |       different device -> account compromised
  +--> Login history: unfamiliar IPs/locations?
  +--> New payment method added? (fraudster added card)
  +--> Rider's location pings at trip time? (rider in NYC, trip in London)
  +--> Driver confirms: rider photo matched account?
  |
  Remediation:
  +--> Refund immediately
  +--> Mark trip as fraudulent
  +--> Ban fraudulent device
  +--> Force password reset + 2FA on rider's account
  +--> Feed signals to fraud detection model
  +--> Pattern analysis: broader attack?
```

sections.title: Q6. The ETA predictions are consistently 30% too low during rush hour. How do you debug and fix?
sections.body:
**Answer:** The ETA model is underestimating traffic. (1) **Verify the data**: pull the last week's trips in the affected city — compare predicted ETA to actual trip duration. Is the 30% bias consistent across all times, or only rush hour? (2) **Model features**: check the ETA model's features — does it include real-time traffic? If it uses only historical averages, rush-hour traffic spikes won't be captured. Add real-time traffic data (driver speed pings aggregated per road segment). (3) **Feature freshness**: if real-time traffic is a feature, is it stale? The Kafka stream of driver pings should update road-segment speeds every 30 s; check Flink job lag. (4) **Model retraining**: when was the model last retrained? Rush-hour patterns change with construction, events, season. If the model is 6 months old, retrain on recent data. (5) **Special events**: was there a one-off event (parade, marathon, sports game) that disrupted traffic? The model can't predict these. (6) **Map data**: if the road network has changed (new road, closed road), the map matching and routing may be wrong. Update the map data. (7) **Dispatch routing**: is the driver being routed through known slow roads? Check the routing service. (8) **Communication to rider**: while debugging, surface a wider ETA range to riders ("8–12 min" instead of "8 min") to set expectations. Fix: add real-time traffic as a feature, retrain the model monthly, and add event-aware overrides. Real-world: Uber's ETA model is a gradient-boosted tree ensemble with hundreds of features including real-time traffic, weather, and events; they retrain continuously.
**Visual:**
```
ETA 30% too low in rush hour
  |
  +--> Verify: predicted vs actual ETA over last week (only rush hour?)
  +--> Model features: includes real-time traffic?
  |       if historical only -> rush-hour spikes missed
  +--> Feature freshness: real-time traffic stale?
  |       Flink lag -> speeds 5 min old
  +--> Model retrained recently? (rush patterns change)
  +--> Special events? (parade, marathon)
  +--> Map data updated? (new/closed roads)
  +--> Routing through slow roads? (check routing svc)
  |
  Fix:
  +--> Add real-time traffic as feature (driver ping speeds per road)
  +--> Retrain monthly
  +--> Add event-aware overrides
  +--> Surface wider ETA range to riders in the meantime
```

sections.title: Q7. The CEO wants to launch self-driving Ubers. How does the architecture change?
sections.body:
**Answer:** Self-driving adds a new actor: the autonomous vehicle (AV) itself, which is both "driver" and "vehicle." Key changes. (1) **AV control service**: a service that monitors each AV's status (online, in-trip, charging, maintenance-needed), receives telemetry (position, speed, obstacle detections, sensor health), and can send commands (pull over, return to depot). Latency must be < 100 ms for safety-critical commands. (2) **Sensor pipeline**: AVs generate gigabytes/s of sensor data (LIDAR, cameras, radar). This data is processed on-vehicle for real-time decisions; a subset is uploaded to the cloud for model retraining and incident analysis (Kafka + S3). (3) **Dispatch**: same algorithm, but AVs have constraints — they can only operate in geofenced "AV-ready" areas (mapped in detail), they need to return to a depot for charging, and they can't pick up certain ride types (e.g., riders with service animals, in some jurisdictions). (4) **Remote assistance**: when an AV encounters a situation it can't handle (construction zone, complex intersection), it calls a remote human operator who takes over via low-latency video link (< 500 ms RTT). A pool of remote operators handles these calls. (5) **Maintenance scheduling**: AVs need frequent cleaning, sensor calibration, and software updates. A scheduling service optimizes when each AV returns to the depot. (6) **Regulatory compliance**: each AV ride must log detailed telemetry for regulatory review (in case of incident). 7-year retention. (7) **Insurance and liability**: AVs shift liability from driver to Uber (or the AV manufacturer). Pricing must account for this. (8) **Rider experience**: rider sees "autonomous vehicle" badge, may have a safety driver initially, can call remote support. Trade-off: AVs are operationally complex but eliminate driver cost (the biggest expense). Real-world: Uber's ATG (Advanced Technologies Group) developed self-driving tech for years; sold to Aurora in 2020 but the architecture remains relevant.
**Visual:**
```
Self-driving Uber architecture changes:
  AV = both "driver" and "vehicle"

New services:
  AV control svc        -> monitor status, send commands (< 100ms)
  Sensor pipeline       -> LIDAR/cameras/radar -> on-vehicle + cloud
  Remote assistance     -> human operator via video link (< 500ms RTT)
  Maintenance scheduling -> depot returns for charging/cleaning
  Regulatory logging    -> detailed telemetry, 7-year retention

Dispatch changes:
  - AVs only in geofenced AV-ready areas
  - Must return to depot for charging
  - Can't pick up certain ride types (service animals, in some areas)

Rider experience:
  - "Autonomous vehicle" badge
  - Safety driver initially
  - Remote support call button

Cost shift:
  - No driver cost (biggest expense eliminated)
  - Higher capex (AV hardware ~$200k/vehicle)
  - Liability shifts from driver to Uber
```
